claim: Clytia jellyfish have tetraradial symmetry.
source: Jellyfish, with their tetraradial symmetry, offer a novel paradigm for addressing patterning mechanisms during regeneration.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and supported by anatomical descriptions and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fragmentation triggers actomyosin-powered remodeling that restores body umbrella shape in Clytia jellyfish.
source: Fragmentation first triggers actomyosin-powered remodeling that restores body umbrella shape, causing radial smooth muscle fibers to converge around 'hubs' which serve as positional landmarks.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing actomyosin cable formation and pharmacological inhibition experiments with blebbistatin.

claim: Radial smooth muscle fibers converge around 'hubs' which serve as positional landmarks during regeneration.
source: Fragmentation first triggers actomyosin-powered remodeling that restores body umbrella shape, causing radial smooth muscle fibers to converge around 'hubs' which serve as positional landmarks.
evidence: Demonstrated through phalloidin staining showing hub formation and correlation with manubrium regeneration sites.

claim: Stabilization of hubs depends on the configuration of the adjoining muscle fiber 'spokes'.
source: Stabilization of these hubs, and associated expression of Wnt6, depends on the configuration of the adjoining muscle fiber 'spokes'.
evidence: Shown through comparison of S and L fragments from bisected jellyfish, where different muscle fiber configurations lead to different hub fates.

claim: Stabilized hubs presage the site of the manubrium blastema.
source: Stabilized hubs presage the site of the manubrium blastema, whose growth is Wnt/β-catenin dependent and fueled by both cell proliferation and long-range cell recruitment.
evidence: Demonstrated by temporal correlation between hub stabilization and blastema formation across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: Manubrium blastema growth is Wnt/β-catenin dependent.
source: Stabilized hubs presage the site of the manubrium blastema, whose growth is Wnt/β-catenin dependent and fueled by both cell proliferation and long-range cell recruitment.
evidence: Supported by PKF118-310 inhibitor experiments blocking manubrium regeneration and Wnt pathway gene expression.

claim: Manubrium blastema growth is fueled by both cell proliferation and long-range cell recruitment.
source: Stabilized hubs presage the site of the manubrium blastema, whose growth is Wnt/β-catenin dependent and fueled by both cell proliferation and long-range cell recruitment.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation experiments and gonad grafting experiments showing cell migration.

claim: Manubrium morphogenesis is modulated by its connections with the gastrovascular canal system.
source: Manubrium morphogenesis is modulated by its connections with the gastrovascular canal system.
evidence: Shown by experiments demonstrating that the number of connected canals determines the number of manubrium lobes.

claim: Body patterning in regenerating jellyfish emerges mainly from local interactions, triggered and directed by the remodeling process.
source: We conclude that body patterning in regenerating jellyfish emerges mainly from local interactions, triggered and directed by the remodeling process.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing lack of long-range morphogen gradients and importance of local structural elements.

claim: All organs (manubrium, gonads, and tentacle bulbs) and radial canals can fully regenerate in Clytia.
source: Firstly, targeted ablations demonstrated that all organs (the feeding manubrium, gonads and tentacle bulbs) and radial canals can fully regenerate (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: Demonstrated through targeted ablation experiments with quantified regeneration outcomes.

claim: Functional manubria regenerated in 4 days.
source: Functional manubria regenerated in 4 days (Figure 1E; n: 43/44)
evidence: Quantified observation from ablation experiments.

claim: Gonads bearing gametes reformed in about a week.
source: while gonads (bearing gametes) and tentacle bulbs reformed in about a week (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; gonads: 48/48, bulbs: 45/52; after 8 days in fed jellyfish).
evidence: Quantified observation from ablation experiments.

claim: Tentacle bulbs reformed in about a week.
source: while gonads (bearing gametes) and tentacle bulbs reformed in about a week (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; gonads: 48/48, bulbs: 45/52; after 8 days in fed jellyfish).
evidence: Quantified observation from ablation experiments.

claim: Removed segments of radial canals rapidly reformed, re-growing from the stumps in both centripetal and centrifugal directions.
source: Removed segments of radial canals rapidly reformed, re-growing from the stumps in both centripetal and centrifugal directions (Figure 1H; notice the growing tip).
evidence: Observed through imaging of regenerating canal tips.

claim: The recovery efficiency of gonads and tentacle bulbs varied, both within and between medusae.
source: The recovery efficiency of gonads and tentacle bulbs varied, both within and between medusae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: Observed variation in regeneration outcomes across experiments.

claim: The manubrium recovered rapidly and stereotypically.
source: while the manubrium recovered rapidly and stereotypically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Quantified observation showing consistent regeneration pattern.

claim: The efficiency of gonad and tentacle bulb regeneration was affected by the feeding regime of the animals.
source: The efficiency of gonad and tentacle bulb regeneration was affected by the feeding regime of the animals, with recovery blocked at an initial stage of cell accumulation in starved animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing fed versus unfed animals in regeneration experiments.

claim: Fragments began remodeling rapidly, reducing the wounded surface, and usually restoring the circular jellyfish shape within 24 hr.
source: Fragments began remodeling rapidly, reducing the wounded surface, and usually restoring the circular jellyfish shape within 24 hr, irrespective of the starting topology and of the number of remaining organs or canals (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed across diverse cutting experiments.

claim: Existing organs and canals are largely conserved during regeneration.
source: Together, the responses to our array of cut topologies indicated that: (i) existing organs and canals are largely conserved
evidence: Inferred from observation of regeneration outcomes across multiple cutting experiments.

claim: The length of the residual circular canal determines the final perimeter of the restored umbrella.
source: (ii) the length of the residual circular canal determines the final perimeter of the restored umbrella
evidence: Inferred from observation of regeneration outcomes across multiple cutting experiments.

claim: The final umbrella size correlates with the amount of tissue in the fragment.
source: (iii) the final umbrella size correlates with the amount of tissue in the fragment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from observation of regeneration outcomes across multiple cutting experiments.

claim: Medusae from which the entire umbrella margin had been removed sealed into a spherical shape and died shortly after.
source: A rare failure in shape restoration concerned medusae from which the entire umbrella margin had been removed (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2T): these fragments sealed into a spherical shape and died shortly after.
evidence: Observed outcome from specific cutting experiment.

claim: If the original four-quadrant body plan had been lost during regeneration, it never recovered.
source: After remodeling and feeding, the umbrella of regenerated jellyfish continued to grow and new tentacle bulbs were added to the circular canal; however, if the original four-quadrant body plan had been lost, it never recovered.
evidence: Observed across long-term monitoring of regenerated jellyfish.

claim: A minority of remodeled manubria sprouted additional radial canals.
source: A minority of remodeled manubria sprouted additional radial canals (6/16 of bisected jellyfish showed a third radial canal after 6 weeks).
evidence: Quantified observation from long-term monitoring.

claim: Following manubrium ablation, the wounded exumbrellar and subumbrellar layers curl and fuse together, sealing off the exposed mesoglea.
source: We characterized the different processes of regeneration as follows: following manubrium ablation (Figures 1E and 2A), the wounded exumbrellar and subumbrellar layers curl and fuse together, sealing off the exposed mesoglea (stage 0, wound closure).
evidence: Observed through time-lapse imaging of regeneration process.

claim: By 12 hpd the tissue gap is closed, and the radial canals meet at the center.
source: By 12 hpd the tissue gap is closed, and the radial canals meet at the center (stage 1, remodeling) and start fusing (n: 10/16 lumen fused at 12 hpd).
evidence: Quantified observation from time-course experiments.

claim: Cells start accumulating at the junction of the radial canals by 12 hpd.
source: Cells start accumulating at the junction of the radial canals, the first sign of organ regeneration; by 24 hpd the cell mass forms a roughly square, flat primordium (stage 2, regeneration primordium).
evidence: Observed through imaging at successive time points.

claim: By 48 hpd the primordium fissures centrally, revealing the gastric cavity.
source: The primordium thickens, and by 48 hpd it fissures centrally, revealing the now distinguishable gastric cavity (stage 3, opening).
evidence: Observed through imaging at successive time points.

claim: Within 4 dpd, the manubrium develops the characteristic lip folds, tetraradially arranged.
source: The protuberance elongates, and within 4 dpd, it develops the characteristic lip folds, tetraradially arranged; the manubrium is now fully functional, albeit smaller than the original one (stage 5, folding) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Observed through imaging at successive time points.

claim: Cell proliferation levels in the subumbrella decreased within the first hours following manubrium ablation.
source: Within the first hours following manubrium ablation, cell proliferation levels in the subumbrella decreased, notably within the segment of radial canal lying between gonad and manubrium (termed 'MG-segment'; Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays at successive time points.

claim: Cell proliferation increased at the regeneration site from 24 hpd.
source: Cell proliferation increased at the regeneration site from 24 hpd, and within the radial canals from 48 hpd.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays at successive time points.

claim: Cell proliferation peaked during primordium thickening stage (72 hpd).
source: Cell proliferation then peaked during primordium thickening stage (72 hpd), before returning to basal levels at 96 hpd (Figure 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays at successive time points.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyurea blocked manubrium regeneration at a pre-opening stage.
source: Treatment with the DNA synthesis inhibitor hydroxyurea blocked manubrium regeneration at a pre-opening stage (stages 2–3), thus establishing the dependency of manubrium outgrowth on cell proliferation (3 days n: 14/20; Figure 2D, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition experiment.

claim: Hydroxyurea treatment did not impair wound healing, umbrella remodeling or the repositioning of regenerating manubrium after bisection.
source: Conversely, hydroxyurea treatment did not impair wound healing, umbrella remodeling or the repositioning of regenerating manubrium after bisection (Figure 2G), consistent with the relatively low number of cells incorporating EdU detected during these processes (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition experiment.

claim: Gonads and tentacle bulbs harbor niches of multipotent stem cells called interstitial stem cells (i-cells).
source: Gonads and tentacle bulbs, which connect to the manubrium via the radial canals, harbor niches of multipotent stem cells (Denker et al., 2008; Leclère et al., 2012) called interstitial stem cells (i-cells; Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and detection of CheNanos1 expression.

claim: Hydrozoan i-cells can generate both somatic and germ cell types.
source: Hydrozoan i-cells can generate both somatic and germ cell types, and along with early precursors of these cell types, express stem cell markers such as Nanos1 (Bosch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In situ hybridization detection of CheNanos1 in manubrium-ablated jellyfish revealed i-cells in both regenerating manubrium and radial canals, starting from 24 hpd.
source: In situ hybridization detection of CheNanos1 in manubrium-ablated jellyfish revealed i-cells (used hereafter in a wide sense to include early precursors of the derivate cell types) in both regenerating manubrium and radial canals, starting from 24 hpd (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: EdU+ cells from grafted gonads were detected in the host medusa both within the regenerating manubrium and in the connecting radial canal around 48 hr after manubrium ablation.
source: Around 48 hr after manubrium ablation, EdU+ cells were detected in the host medusa both within the regenerating manubrium and in the connecting radial canal (Figure 3D, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: Demonstrated by gonad grafting experiment with EdU labeling.

claim: A subpopulation of the migrating EdU+ cells expressed CheNanos1.
source: A subpopulation of the migrating EdU+ cells expressed CheNanos1 (Figure 3E, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: Demonstrated by double labeling with EdU and CheNanos1 FISH.

claim: EdU+/CheNanos1+ cells were found exclusively in the MG-segment of radial canals and in the manubrium primordium.
source: EdU+/CheNanos1+ cells were found exclusively in the MG-segment of radial canals and in the manubrium primordium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–I), indicating that cell migration from the gonad is directed towards the regeneration site.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of EdU/CheNanos1 double-positive cell distribution.

claim: Small oocytes labeled by EdU were detected both in the radial canal and regenerating primordium.
source: Unexpectedly, small oocytes (significantly larger than the CheNanos1+ i-cells) labeled by EdU were also detected both in the radial canal and regenerating primordium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Observed in gonad grafting experiments.

claim: No mobilization of EdU+/CheNanos1+ cells from the gonad was observed in undamaged medusae.
source: No mobilization of EdU+/CheNanos1+ cells from the gonad was observed in undamaged medusae (Figure 3F–H), suggesting that cellular recruitment is triggered by the regeneration process.
evidence: Demonstrated by control experiments with grafted gonads in non-regenerating hosts.

claim: Mobilizing Gastro-Digestive (MGD) cells are characterized by brown pigmentation and circulate actively in the canals during regeneration.
source: We noted another cell type, characterized by brown pigmentation, which circulated actively in the canals during regeneration and appeared to integrate into the manubrium primordium.
evidence: Observed through live imaging and fluorescent bead labeling.

claim: MGD cells were detected in the gastroderm of manubrium, gonads and tentacle bulbs in undamaged jellyfish.
source: In undamaged jellyfish, these cells were detected in the gastroderm of manubrium, gonads and tentacle bulbs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed through imaging of undamaged jellyfish.

claim: MGD cells can be specifically labeled by feeding the medusa with fluorescent beads.
source: We could label them specifically by feeding the medusa with fluorescent beads (Figure 4A, see Methods), supporting the idea that they function in nutrient uptake, and that the brown pigmentation derives from the crustacean diet (Artemia nauplii).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescent bead feeding experiments.

claim: MGD cells circulated rapidly within the lumen of the radial canal following manubrium ablation.
source: These previously undescribed cells, which we term Mobilizing Gastro-Digestive (MGD) cells circulated rapidly within the lumen of the radial canal following manubrium ablation, likely transported by the flagellar beating of canal gastrodermal cells that govern nutrient flow (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed through time-lapse imaging.

claim: Some of the gastrodermal cells of the regenerating manubrium originated from other organs of the jellyfish.
source: Analysis of bead-labeled jellyfish following manubrium dissection revealed that some of the gastrodermal cells of the regenerating manubrium did indeed originate from other organs of the jellyfish (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescent bead labeling and tracking experiments.

claim: MGD cells from the gonad gastroderm are recruited to the primordium of the regenerating manubrium.
source: Transplantation of a gonad from a medusa fed with fluorescent beads to an unlabeled host prior to manubrium ablation confirmed that MGD cells from the gonad gastroderm are recruited to the primordium of the regenerating manubrium, as well as to other non-regenerating bulbs and non-dissected manubria (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by gonad grafting experiment with fluorescent bead labeling.

claim: MGD cells can be recruited from tentacle bulbs when gonads are removed.
source: In medusae from which all gonads had been removed, fluorescent bead-labelled MGD cells were detected in the manubrium primordium once the radial canals had regrown, showing that these cells can be recruited not only from gonads but also from more peripheral regions, likely from the gastroderm of the tentacle bulbs (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by experiment with gonad removal and fluorescent bead labeling.

claim: MGD cells travel uniquely through the gastrodermal canal system.
source: On the other hand, no fluorescent bead-labelled MGD cells were found in the manubrium primordium if both gonads and radial canals were completely ablated (Figure 4F). This demonstrates that MGD cells travel uniquely through the gastrodermal canal system.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiment with complete canal ablation.

claim: Intact radial canals are necessary for manubrium regeneration.
source: Related experiments demonstrated that intact radial canals are necessary for manubrium regeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments removing radial canals.

claim: Removal of all four radial canals led either to stalling of regeneration at early stages or to formation of abnormal manubria.
source: The removal of all four radial canals (including gonads), leaving just their most proximal segments intact, led either to stalling of regeneration at early stages (stages 2–3, open cavity) or to formation of abnormal manubria with incorrect geometry and disrupted morphogenesis, notably lacking the deep folds shaping the four edges of the manubrium column (Figures 4F and 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by canal ablation experiments.

claim: Correct morphogenesis of a manubrium only occurred when at least one radial canal was connected to the peripheral gastrovascular system.
source: Correct morphogenesis of a manubrium only occurred when at least one radial canal was connected to the peripheral gastrovascular system (Figure 5B), with the details of its morphology conditioned by the number of canals (see below).
evidence: Demonstrated by canal ablation and reconnection experiments.

claim: The number of lobes of the regenerating manubrium always reflected the number of remaining radial canals.
source: Furthermore, irrespective of the dissection topology, the number of lobes of the regenerating manubrium always reflected the number of remaining radial canals, such that three radial canals generated a three-lobed manubrium, and so on (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by systematic manipulation of canal number.

claim: The topology of the regenerating manubrium is determined by the number of connecting canals.
source: We conclude that the topology of the regenerating manubrium is determined by the number of connecting canals, which might provide a mechanical or biochemical signal, and/or might materially contribute to the primordium composition by providing migrating cells (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments manipulating canal number.

claim: Canal fragments connected to the primordium but not to any other organ were sufficient to direct the geometry of the regenerated manubrium.
source: Arguing against the latter option, canal fragments connected to the primordium but not to any other organ were found to be sufficient to direct the geometry of the regenerated manubrium (Figure 5B), as long as at least one canal remained connected to other organs (gonads and/or bulbs).
evidence: Demonstrated by specific canal ablation experiment.

claim: The initial position of the manubrium anlage does not necessarily coincide with the geometrical center of the remodeled medusa.
source: In regenerates, the initial position of the manubrium anlage does not necessarily coincide with the geometrical center of the remodeled medusa (e.g. in quarter jellyfish fragments; Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in quarter fragment experiments.

claim: The manubrium anlage was invariably associated with radial canal(s) and an aggregate ('hub') of smooth muscle fibers.
source: The anlage was, however, invariably associated with radial canal(s) and an aggregate ('hub') of smooth muscle fibers.
evidence: Observed across all regeneration experiments.

claim: Complete manubrium regeneration is dependent on the presence of radial canals.
source: Experiments presented above showed that complete manubrium regeneration is dependent on the presence of radial canals.
evidence: Demonstrated by canal ablation experiments.

claim: Interradial fragments lacking a radial canal showed no signs of primordium formation at 4 dpd.
source: Consistently, interradial fragments lacking a radial canal showed no signs of primordium formation at 4 dpd (Figure 6B).
evidence: Observed in interradial fragment experiments.

claim: After two weeks, a simple tube-like manubrium (unable to feed) was observed in a few interradial fragments lacking radial canals.
source: After two weeks, however, a simple tube-like manubrium (unable to feed) was observed in a few cases (n: 13/65; Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantified observation from long-term monitoring of interradial fragments.

claim: Primordia and regenerated manubria were systematically associated with the aggregate (hub) of smooth muscle fibers that formed during the remodeling process.
source: Strikingly, F-actin staining showed that primordia and regenerated manubria were systematically associated with the aggregate (hub) of smooth muscle fibers that formed during the remodeling process (Figure 6A; n: 22/22).
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin staining across multiple experiments.

claim: A muscle hub could be detected before the anlage formed, irrespective of the wound topology.
source: In all cases, a muscle hub could be detected before the anlage formed (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), irrespective of the wound topology.
evidence: Observed through time-course imaging across multiple wound topologies.

claim: Hub formation did not require radial canals.
source: Hub formation did not require radial canals, since it was unaffected by removal of the MG-segment of radial canals after manubrium excision (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by canal ablation experiment.

claim: Manubrium regeneration commenced when at least one of the excised canals regrew to the hub of smooth muscle fibers.
source: In those canal-ablated medusae, manubrium regeneration commenced when at least one of the excised canals regrew to the hub of smooth muscle fibers (Figure 6C; primordium on hub at 4 dpd: 8/9; manubrium at the center of umbrella at 5 dpd: 18/18).
evidence: Quantified observation from canal ablation and regrowth experiments.

claim: A longitudinal deep cut through the umbrella of manubrium-ablated medusae resulted in the formation of two separate manubria primordia.
source: In order to test the relationship between the muscle fibers hub and the site of manubrium regeneration, we performed a longitudinal deep cut through the umbrella of manubrium-ablated medusae (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). This cut topology disrupted the wound closure and remodeling processes, resulting in the formation of two separate manubria primordia (Figure 6D; n: 34/105, at 24 hpd) located on two muscle hubs (n: 13/16).
evidence: Quantified observation from double-cut experiment.

claim: Grafted manubria could co-exist stably with the original one.
source: We tested this hypothesis by grafting supernumerary manubria at different subumbrellar positions. Grafted manubria could co-exist stably with the original one (Figure 7A), with each manubrium behaving independently and participating in feeding.
evidence: Demonstrated by manubrium grafting experiments.

claim: Grafted manubria rapidly sprouted new canals, which reconnected to the existing gastrovascular system.
source: The grafted manubria rapidly sprouted new canals, which reconnected to the existing gastrovascular system (Figure 7A).
evidence: Observed in manubrium grafting experiments.

claim: Grafting a fragment of a manubrium base onto the umbrella tissues systematically led to its regeneration into a functional extra manubrium.
source: Grafting a fragment of a manubrium base onto the umbrella tissues, either on a radial canal or directly adjacent to the endogenous manubrium, systematically led to its regeneration into a functional extra manubrium (Figure 7B; tubular/bi-lobed shape: 12/12).
evidence: Quantified observation from manubrium fragment grafting experiments.

claim: Manubria grafted on the radial canal or the umbrella did not prevent the regeneration of an excised manubrium.
source: Furthermore, manubria grafted either on the radial canal (Figure 7C) or the umbrella (Figure 7D) did not prevent the regeneration of an excised manubrium, resulting in the formation of a two-manubria medusa (n: 10/10 and 17/20, respectively).
evidence: Quantified observation from grafting experiments.

claim: No regeneration occurred when exogenous manubria were grafted adjacent to the excised one.
source: In contrast, no regeneration occurred when exogenous manubria were grafted adjacent to the excised one (Figure 7E; n: 15/20).
evidence: Quantified observation from grafting experiments.

claim: Existing manubria can exert only a local inhibition on manubrium reformation.
source: These experiments indicate that existing manubria can exert only a local inhibition on manubrium reformation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from grafting experiments showing distance-dependent effects.

claim: Grafted manubria provoked a local reorganization of smooth muscle fibers, which converged towards the grafted manubrium.
source: The organization of muscle fibers in manubrium-grafted jellyfish provided a possible explanation for the observed short-range inhibitory influence (Figure 7F–H). Grafted manubria appeared to provoke a local reorganization of smooth muscle fibers, which converged towards the grafted manubrium (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: Observed through phalloidin staining in grafting experiments.

claim: When grafted manubria were positioned close to the ablation site, the smooth muscle fibers were not arranged in a hub at the ablation site.
source: Significantly, in cases where the grafted manubria were positioned close to the ablation site of the endogenous manubrium (resulting in an inhibition of its regeneration), the smooth muscle fibers were not arranged in a hub at the ablation site, but laid parallel to the wound site.
evidence: Observed through phalloidin staining in grafting experiments.

claim: A continuous bundle of actin lined the remodeling edge in all cases.
source: Wound closure progressively constricts injured tissues, drawing together the intact parts (Figure 8A–C). In all cases, a continuous bundle of actin lined the remodeling edge (Figure 8F), reminiscent of the actin ring described around wound sites in the exumbrella layer of Clytia (Kamran et al., 2017).
evidence: Observed through phalloidin staining across multiple wound types.

claim: Phosphorylated (activated) Myosin Regulatory Light Chain 2 (MRLC) was detected around the wound area.
source: Detection of phosphorylated (activated) Myosin Regulatory Light Chain 2 (MRLC) around the wound area by antibody staining (Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) is consistent with local activation of the actomyosin contraction system.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining with phospho-MRLC antibody.

claim: Treatment with myosin II inhibitors impaired umbrella remodeling.
source: Treatment with myosin II inhibitors (such as blebbistatin or BDM) impaired umbrella remodeling, providing further evidence that the forces that underpin remodeling of the umbrella result from actomyosin activity (Figure 8H and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Remodeling is accompanied by localized reorganization of both the subumbrellar radial muscle layer and of the underlying mesoglea.
source: Staining of F-actin and tracing using the vital dye DiI demonstrated that remodeling is accompanied by localized reorganization of both the subumbrellar radial muscle layer (Figure 8B,C) and of the underlying mesoglea (Figure 8D,E), reorganization that is limited to the area proximal to the wound.
evidence: Demonstrated by phalloidin staining and DiI tracing experiments.

claim: During the constriction phase, the radial alignment of smooth muscle fibers loosened and they partially disorganized.
source: During the constriction phase (1–12 hpd), the radial alignment of smooth muscle fibers loosened and they partially disorganized (Figure 8B; 6 hpd), recovering a radial orientation later (12–24 hpd) (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Observed through time-course phalloidin staining.

claim: Treatment with menthol did not prevent remodeling of bisected medusae, inducing only a slight delay.
source: Treatment with the anesthetic menthol, which efficiently blocks umbrella contractions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), did not prevent remodeling of bisected medusae, inducing only a slight delay of remodeling (Figure 8I).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological treatment experiment.

claim: Rhythmic contractions of the striated muscle are not necessary to the remodeling process in Clytia.
source: Thus rhythmic contractions of the striated muscle are not necessary to the remodeling process in Clytia.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from menthol treatment experiments.

claim: In the S-fragment, smooth muscle fibers converged towards the 'hub' site, maintaining their connections to the margin of the umbrella, evolving into a stable radial hub structure.
source: In the S-fragment, smooth muscle fibers subsequently started to converge towards the 'hub' site, maintaining their connections to the margin of the umbrella. This characteristic topology evolved into a stable radial hub structure, which was then translated towards the new geometrical center of the umbrella, prefiguring the appearance of a manubrium primordium (Figure 9A).
evidence: Observed through time-course phalloidin staining of S fragments.

claim: In the L-fragment, the severed fibers that gathered into the initial hub adopted a parallel arrangement, and the hub figure displaced away from the wound site and disappeared.
source: In the L-fragment, the severed fibers that gathered into the initial hub had a different organization and instead adopted a parallel arrangement, all being connected at one end to the wound site and at the other extremity to the manubrium (Figure 9B). During subsequent re-centering of the manubrium, this hub figure displaced away from the wound site, and the surrounding fibers reoriented to reestablish the original configuration around the endogenous manubrium, while the wound-induced hub disappeared (Figure 9B).
evidence: Observed through time-course phalloidin staining of L fragments.

claim: The stabilization of a wound-induced hub depends on the configuration of the connecting muscle fibers.
source: We propose a model where the stabilization of a wound-induced hub depends on the configuration of the connecting muscle fibers: stabilization of the muscle hub occurs when the fibers are not constrained by attachment to an existing hub.
evidence: Model proposed based on observations from S/L fragment experiments.

claim: Transcript levels of Wnt-pathway components and of known downstream targets modulated dynamically during the regeneration process.
source: Transcript levels of Wnt-pathway components and of known downstream targets (CheBra1 and CheFoxA, see Lapébie et al., 2014) modulated dynamically during the regeneration process (Figure 10B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis at successive time points.

claim: Most of Clytia Wnt genes were found to be expressed highly in the non-dissected manubrium and lowly in the surrounding umbrella tissues.
source: Most of Clytia Wnt genes were found to be expressed highly in the non-dissected manubrium (n.d.), and lowly in the surrounding umbrella tissues (0 hpd) (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq and in situ hybridization.

claim: Wnt gene expression increased during manubrium regeneration.
source: Their expression then increased during manubrium regeneration (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq and in situ hybridization at successive time points.

claim: CheWnt6 and Cheβ-cat were activated early at the constricting wound area (6 hpd).
source: In situ hybridization revealed that, following manubrium excision, CheWnt6 and Cheβ-cat were activated early at the constricting wound area (6 hpd), while transcripts for CheWnt3 and the Wnt-pathway downstream targets CheBra1 and CheFoxA started to be detectable later at the 'hub' site (24–48 hpd; Figure 10B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization at successive time points.

claim: CheWnt3, CheBra1 and CheFoxA transcripts started to be detectable later at the 'hub' site (24–48 hpd).
source: In situ hybridization revealed that, following manubrium excision, CheWnt6 and Cheβ-cat were activated early at the constricting wound area (6 hpd), while transcripts for CheWnt3 and the Wnt-pathway downstream targets CheBra1 and CheFoxA started to be detectable later at the 'hub' site (24–48 hpd; Figure 10B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization at successive time points.

claim: CheAxin expression could first be detected at the hub/blastema site from 48 hpd.
source: Expression of CheAxin, a modulator of canonical Wnt signaling, could first be detected at the hub/blastema site from 48 hpd (Figure 10C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization.

claim: Treatment with PKF118-310 blocked regeneration of manubrium prior to blastema development.
source: Treatment of injured jellyfish (from 17 hpd until 48 hpd) with PKF118-310, a chemical inhibitor of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, blocked regeneration of manubrium prior to blastema development ('stages 1–2' in Figure 10D).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition experiment.

claim: PKF118-310 treatment of Clytia embryos phenocopied the strong 'aboralization' obtained following CheWnt3 knockdown.
source: Inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signaling by PKF118-310 was validated using Clytia embryos, where the role of this pathway in axis development is well characterized (Momose et al., 2008; Lapébie et al., 2014). 21 hr treatments, starting from cleavage stage, phenocopied the strong 'aboralization' obtained following CheWnt3 knockdown (Momose et al., 2008).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological treatment of embryos and comparison to published knockdown phenotypes.

claim: Treatment with PKF118-310 prevented expression of Wnt-pathway components and downstream targets at the hub.
source: In dissected jellyfish, treatment with PKF118-310 prevented expression of Wnt-pathway components and downstream targets (CheWnt3, CheWnt6, CheBra1, CheFoxA, CheAxin) at the hub, as shown by in situ hybridization (Figure 10C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization in PKF118-310 treated jellyfish.

claim: qPCR experiments showed a strong reduction of the target genes (CheBra1, CheFoxA) following PKF118-310 treatment.
source: qPCR experiments showed a strong reduction of the target genes (CheBra1, CheFoxA), a milder reduction for some pathway components (CheWnt3, CheAxin), and no significant reduction for the early-expressed genes CheWnt6 and Cheβ-cat (Figure 10E).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR analysis.

claim: When PKF118-310 treatment commenced immediately after dissection, it strongly delayed wound closure.
source: When PKF118-310 treatment commenced immediately after dissection, it strongly delayed wound closure, suggesting that Wnt/β-catenin signaling may also be involved in early phases of remodeling.
evidence: Observed in pharmacological treatment experiments.

claim: CheWnt6 expression was detected at the remodeling wound site of both S and L fragments at 8 hpd.
source: In situ hybridization on 'S' and 'L' fragments from bisected medusae revealed an early activation of CheWnt6 expression on both 'sides' of the remodeling wound (8 hpd; Figure 11A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization on S and L fragments.

claim: CheWnt6 expression became undetectable by in situ hybridization in L fragments at 24 hpd, while it reinforced in the S fragments.
source: Following the subsequent disassembly of the hub in the larger fragments, CheWnt6 expression became undetectable by in situ hybridization in L fragments, while it reinforced in the S fragments, where hubs were stabilized (24 hpd; Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization on S and L fragments at 24 hpd.

claim: Inhibition of remodeling with blebbistatin suppressed CheWnt6-expression in both S and L fragments.
source: Inhibition of remodeling with blebbistatin suppressed CheWnt6-expression in both S and L fragments (at 8 hpd and 24 hpd; Figure 11A,C)
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization in blebbistatin-treated fragments.

claim: CheWnt6 signal was detected at the remodeling wound site (at 24 hpd) following 9 hr of blebbistatin washout, in both S and L fragments.
source: while CheWnt6 signal was detected at the remodeling wound site (at 24 hpd) following 9 hr of inhibitor washout, in both S and L fragments (Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization after blebbistatin washout.

claim: qPCR quantification revealed a much stronger upregulation (>100-fold) of CheWnt6 in the remodeling wound area of untreated S fragments at 8 hpd compared to blebbistatin-treated S fragments (2- to 4-fold).
source: qPCR quantification revealed a much stronger upregulation (>100-fold) of CheWnt6 in the remodeling wound area of untreated S fragments at 8 hpd (Figure 11C and Figure 11—figure supplement 1) compared to the relaxed wound area of blebbistatin-treated S fragments (2- to 4-fold) (Figure 11C and Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR analysis comparing control and blebbistatin-treated fragments.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment caused an unexpected generalized increase in CheWnt6 expression in the umbrella tissues of both non-dissected and injured jellyfish.
source: Blebbistatin treatment also caused an unexpected generalized increase in CheWnt6 expression in the umbrella tissues of both non-dissected and injured jellyfish (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through qPCR analysis of blebbistatin-treated samples.

claim: Expression of Wnt6 is strongly and rapidly activated during actomyosin-dependent wound remodeling in Clytia.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that expression of Wnt6 is strongly and rapidly activated during actomyosin-dependent wound remodeling in Clytia, and later maintained at the stabilized muscle hub.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in situ hybridization and qPCR experiments with and without blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling becomes necessary for later stages of manubrium regeneration.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling becomes necessary for later stages of manubrium regeneration.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from PKF118-310 inhibitor experiments.

claim: The manubrium of Clytia medusae does not act as an organizer of global patterning.
source: The manubrium of Clytia medusae, unlike the hypostome of Hydra polyps, thus does not appear to act as an organizer of global patterning.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from grafting experiments showing lack of long-range inhibition.

claim: The manubrium can be considered the pivotal element of a self-organizing system based on local interactions.
source: Rather it can be considered the pivotal element of a self-organizing system based on local interactions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Clytia jellyfish are made up of four identical morphological units, called quadrants.
source: Clytia jellyfish are made up of four identical morphological units, called quadrants.
evidence: Stated as anatomical description.

claim: Each umbrellar quadrant harbors one radial gastrovascular canal, a gonad, one lobe of the tetraradially-organized manubrium and a segment of the circular peripheral canal connecting the tentacle bulbs.
source: Each umbrellar quadrant harbors one radial gastrovascular canal, a gonad, one lobe of the tetraradially-organized manubrium (Figure 1D) and a segment of the circular peripheral canal connecting the tentacle bulbs (up to four per quadrant).
evidence: Stated as anatomical description with supporting figure.

claim: The manubrium, tentacle bulbs and gonads harbor populations of stem cells.
source: The manubrium, tentacle bulbs and gonads harbor populations of stem cells (Amiel and Houliston, 2009; Denker et al., 2008; Leclère et al., 2012), have autonomous functions and can be regarded as true organs.
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The main component of the umbrella is an acellular connective layer, the mesoglea.
source: The main component of the umbrella is an acellular connective layer, the mesoglea (Figure 1C), covered on its external surface, the 'exumbrella', by a simple monolayer of epithelial cells (Kamran et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as anatomical description with citation.

claim: The concave face of the umbrella, termed 'subumbrella', is composed of three overlapping tissues layers.
source: The concave face of the umbrella, termed 'subumbrella', is composed of three overlapping tissues layers (Figure 1C): (i) an inner epithelium associated with the mesoglea, (ii) an overlying cnidarian-specific tissue type comprising radially aligned smooth epitheliomuscular cells ('radial smooth muscles'), (iii) a ring of striated epitheliomuscular cells at the umbrella periphery which power swimming contractions, and are sandwiched between the other two layers (Leclère and Röttinger, 2016).
evidence: Stated as anatomical description with citation.

claim: Studies using wild-collected hydrozoan jellyfish concluded that a high proportion of individuals had undergone regeneration following damages caused by predation.
source: Studies using wild-collected hydrozoan jellyfish, notably of the genus Clytia, concluded that a high proportion of individuals had undergone regeneration following damages caused by predation (Mills, 1993).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: A recent study showed that lost parts are not replaced in Aurelia juveniles following amputation, although rotational symmetry is restored by a muscle-powered process termed 'symmetrization'.
source: A recent study showed that lost parts are not replaced in Aurelia juveniles following amputation, although rotational symmetry is restored by a muscle-powered process termed 'symmetrization' (Abrams et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Clytia is now a reliable laboratory model with extensive genomic and transcriptomic resources.
source: Clytia is now a reliable laboratory model with extensive genomic and transcriptomic resources (Houliston et al., 2010; Leclère et al., 2019), amenable to gene function analyses (Momose et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The complex life cycle of Clytia, comprising two adult phases - the polyp and the medusa - can be completed reliably in the laboratory.
source: The complex life cycle, comprising two adult phases - the polyp and the medusa - can be completed reliably in the laboratory (Houliston et al., 2010; Lechable et al., 2019)
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Clytia medusae show 4-fold rotational symmetry around the central feeding organ, termed the manubrium.
source: Clytia medusae show 4-fold rotational symmetry around the central feeding organ, termed the manubrium (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Stated as anatomical description with supporting figures.

claim: In Hydra polyps, the mouth (hypostome) acts as a signaling center and the source of a morphogen gradient organizing the body axis.
source: In hydrozoan polyps, the mouth (hypostome) acts as a signaling center and the source of a morphogen gradient organizing the body axis (e.g. Bode, 2009; Mayorova et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Morphogen gradients are not responsible for the positioning and regeneration of manubria in Clytia jellyfish.
source: In contrast, morphogen gradients are not responsible for the positioning and regeneration of manubria in Clytia jellyfish, as shown by our grafting experiments and the pioneering work of Schmid et al., 1976.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from grafting experiments and comparison to previous work.

claim: The angular position of elements around the oral-aboral body axis is not encoded by a system of rotational coordinates, but depends rather on cues from existing structures.
source: Our findings demonstrate that, in regenerating animals, the angular position of elements around this body axis is not encoded by a system of rotational coordinates, but depends rather on cues from existing structures.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The characteristic tetraradial symmetry of the adult jellyfish does not depend on an actively maintained global patterning system.
source: The characteristic tetraradial symmetry of the adult jellyfish thus does not depend on an actively maintained global patterning system.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from regeneration experiments showing loss of symmetry.

claim: Missing gonads reform at their original location along the radial canal.
source: We cannot nevertheless exclude that a system of morphogen might be secondarily patterning the centro-peripheral axis: missing gonads, for instance, reform at their original location along the radial canal.
evidence: Observed in regeneration experiments.

claim: 'Spoke and hub' muscle configurations can be recognized during wound healing/regeneration in Hydra polyps and planarians.
source: 'Spoke and hub' muscle configurations equivalent to the one we describe here in Clytia can also be recognized during wound healing/regeneration in Hydra polyps (Livshits et al., 2017) and planarians (Scimone et al., 2017), even though they have not been pointed out explicitly.
evidence: Inferred from comparison to published work on other organisms.

claim: 'Spoke and hub' patterning systems might represent a general but overlooked feature of regenerating animals.
source: 'Spoke and hub' patterning systems might thus represent a general but overlooked feature of regenerating animals, playing an early role in the stabilization of remodeling tissues and acting as 'organizers', accurately positioning structures in broadly perturbed systems.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from observations in Clytia and comparison to other organisms.
